AI Mode reply for python asyncio timeout

In Python, you can enforce timeouts on asynchronous operations using asyncio.timeout() (recommended for Python 3.11+) or asyncio.wait_for(). Both mechanisms cancel the running operation and raise a built-in TimeoutError if the time limit expires. 
1. asyncio.timeout() (Python 3.11+)
This context manager is the modern, preferred way to wrap one or multiple await calls in a single timeout block. 
python
import asyncio

async def fetch_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    return "Done"

async def main():
    try:
        # Cancel the block if it takes longer than 2 seconds
        async with asyncio.timeout(2.0):
            result = await fetch_data()
            print(result)
    except TimeoutError:
        print("Operation timed out!")

asyncio.run(main())
Use code with caution.
Copy code text to clipboard.
  • Dynamic deadlines. You can pass None to start without a timeout and set or update it later using cm.reschedule(deadline). 
  • Absolute time. Use asyncio.timeout_at(when) if you want to specify an exact event-loop clock timestamp (loop.time() + seconds) instead of a relative delay. 
2. asyncio.wait_for() (All Python 3 versions)
If you need compatibility with Python 3.10 or older—or only want to wrap a single awaitable—use asyncio.wait_for(). 
python
import asyncio

async def fetch_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)
    return "Done"

async def main():
    try:
        result = await asyncio.wait_for(fetch_data(), timeout=2.0)
        print(result)
    except TimeoutError:  # Note: asyncio.TimeoutError is an alias for TimeoutError
        print("Operation timed out!")

asyncio.run(main())
Use code with caution.

Quick Comparison
Featureasyncio.timeout()asyncio.wait_for()
Python Version3.11+3.4+ (All modern versions)
Syntaxasync with blockWraps a single coroutine/task
Multi-step blocksYes (covers everything inside the block)No (requires wrapping in a helper coroutine)
ReschedulableYes, via .reschedule()No
Key Caveats
  • Always catch TimeoutError outside the block. Internally, asyncio.timeout() cancels the task with asyncio.CancelledError and converts it into TimeoutError when exiting the async with block. Catching TimeoutError inside the block will not work. 
  • Clean up resources in finally. Because timeouts work via task cancellation, put cleanup logic (like closing files or connections) in a try...finally block inside your coroutine. 
  • Protect critical tasks with asyncio.shield(). If you want a timeout to stop waiting for a task without actually cancelling it in the background, wrap the coroutine in asyncio.shield(). 
Check out the Python asyncio documentation for more details on task cancellation and timeout edge cases.
